utterances.text: About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you proceed? Did you do only one copy of each selected document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. With regard to the documents the Tribunal obtained, I made two copies, one copy for the Tribunal and one which I added, as it were, to the folders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What do you mean to the folders? Each one to the relative folder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have a folder. I'd copy the documents there and I'd put the originals back into the folder, and the other documents I kept outside the folder. I put them on top, I think. There were 12, I believe, folders all together, but it was only some folders that had documents in them that were copied, and I made, as I said, two copies, one for the Tribunal, one for us, and then the folders were given numbers. It said "I" for INDA-BAU. Then they were numbered 1 through 12. The individual pages were not numbered at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So if I didn't misunderstand you, for each selected document you did a copy for the ICTY people and a copy which you put in the pertinent folder, together with the -- on the pertinent folder, together with the original; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the folder; on the folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did you give to the ICTY officers their photocopies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all was done right away. I got a folder, made the copies, went back and gave the copies to the person in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: By the way, was any of the ICTY officers present with you at the photocopying operations, of this photocopying operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you personally do after these photocopying operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after the copies were finished, the people from the Tribunal left. I don't know what they did then. I was in the room briefly, so 7.30 the Niederschrift had already begun with Mucic. It was Borlak who were working on that. I was just there on and off. Then about 8.30 pm, after the Niederschrift -- there's two parts to it. There's about the individual part and then there's about the case. It was Borlak who began the first part. Then as of 8.30 I took over with the -- about the case part of the record, the Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean that the ICTY people were not there any more at the beginning of the police interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not there when we took this down for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So did the police interview with Mr. Mucic take place in the same room, 331?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So, as I understand, you did not take part from the beginning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there on an on-and-off basis. I wasn't there when it was started. Then I was back in the room then I'd step out for a minute, and when the document got to the -- about the case part, that's when I took over and I was there from then on until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So who did inform Mucic about his rights right at the beginning of the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would have been Borlak who would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon for a second, your Honour. Mr. Moerbauer, can you tell the court which are the rights a suspect must be informed of by the Austrian police officers at the beginning of a police interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was being questioned as an accused person, and as such he need not speak, but he does have the possibility to make statements. Those statements will be used before a court. Should he proceed with a confession, that would be grounds for mitigation. That is provided for in the law. Then he also had the possibility of notifying a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He need not say anything that might incriminate a relative, etc. So that's the basis for not speaking, and he is advised to speak the truth. Now when it comes to the Niederschriften records, he may lie to me. I'm not in a judicial authority, so that's not punishable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbauer, after you have joined the interviewing team --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. You also tell him: "You can tell a lie to me", a police officer when interrogating an accused telling him: "You can tell a lie to me"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he is told to tell the truth but the bottom line is it doesn't matter if he tells the truth or not. There's no consequences, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is our civil law system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what he said, that he was told he can tell a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: After you joined the interviewing team who were the persons present in the room and who were the persons taking part in the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to about the case part, I went ahead with the questioning. The interpreter was there, Ms. Supput. Also in the office most of the time Panzer was there and at times Gschwendt was there and Bycek, Borlak kept coming in as well, but with regard to the questions relating to the case, I put those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At what time was the interview finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 1 o'clock, but -- well, rather at the beginning -- rather, the beginning and the end of the interview are indicated on the record, on the Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there any break in the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any break, but Mr. Mucic was provided with drinks and coffee. He didn't want anything to eat, but at 1.15, when he was handed over to the court, I went with him and he was given a sandwich and an apple by Panzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. So who were the persons who signed the interview record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The record was signed by Mucic, by the interpreter and by all of the people who were present during the interview. Even if they were only there briefly, they still signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Moerbauer. What did you do right after the end of this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took Mucic to the 9th District to the prison there and he was transferred to the prison authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you bring Mr. Mucic there? Did you drive there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We drove there with an official vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to say some words, to talk to Mr. Mucic during the drive to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We told him we were taking him to the detention centre the following day. He already knew that, but that he would be questioned by the investigating judge, and we talked to him just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In which language did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In German.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he give some answer? Did he say something to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He doesn't speak excellent German, but it's good enough to make himself understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion to see Mr. Mucic again after this in the following days or weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion to see again the ICTY officers in the following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 20th March a South African, I think Dutoit, was in the office and received the copies of the videotapes from Mucic's apartment, and there was a call by Bycek to the court and Dr Seda was told that the tapes had been copied and that Mr. Dutoit was there and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With respect, your Honour, he is relating a conversation by some completely different person. Was he present during this conversation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was present during that telephone call. Dutoit was in the office and Dutoit also spoke to the examining magistrate and subsequently Bycek filled out a document saying that Dr Seda would be handed over, and it was noted down that Dr Seda had received a written request to send a written approval. Dr Seda said he didn't have time to do that and that we should note down in our document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally have a conversation with this officer of ICTY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but just about work in a general way of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did this person remain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Half an hour. Was there any other occasion for you to see any of the ICTY officers after this short visit and in the immediate following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about all the original seized material? Where was it kept in custody after the seizure and in the following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The seized material was in the boxes, in a sports bag, and the boxes were put in a cabinet that could be locked in the office. That's where they were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever photocopy the seized document entirely for your police file in the following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the police records, yes, the relevant documents were copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you proceed personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before the translation work was done I copied all the documents, that is to say in the week following the arrest. We started in part on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So was this photocopying of the entire bunch of relevant matter done the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the next or the day after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We understand that the majority of the written documents were contained, as you said, in one folder seized in Mr. Delalic's apartment and in 12 folders seized in the INDA-BAU premises. Did you photocopy the documents contained in all these files for your personal police file?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A large part. There were some notes of things that were illegible. We didn't copy that. So sometimes you just have notes with scribbling on them, and we didn't copy things that were in another folder. There were some things that were quite sizeable and we knew that they were in other folders, so we didn't make another copy of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you organise this -- I mean, did you organise the photocopies for your file in the same order and dividing them in the same way as the originals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you examine thoroughly the whole seized material in the following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was looked at thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was that done by you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the presence of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you instructed by Mr. Gschwendt to perform this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you start examining the videotapes or the written documents or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started with the video cassettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So how did you proceed with the video cassettes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we took the tapes and we played them at fast speed, and we looked to see whether there was any mistreatment that had been filmed on the tape. Then some notes were made about the contents of the tape. That was written by hand. Then subsequently that was put in a more formal document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see from the transcript you say "we took the tapes and we played." Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other officers also looked at tapes as well. I saw some 60 tapes myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you watch the videos together with an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we weren't concerned about the sound track. We wanted to know whether any mistreatment had been filmed. At the time it wasn't that relevant for us to know what the sound track might be about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did that take, to examine all these seized videotapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Viewing the tapes took one and a half to two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In which day did you start examining these videotapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The following day we already got underway with viewing the videotapes. On the first day not many could be seen because we only have one VCR and there were the tapes that had to be made for the Tribunal. After that it speeded up considerably, because they could be viewed at fast speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say that the work took between one week and a half and two weeks, do you mean you worked full-time or part-time on the videotapes watching?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most of the time was spent on videotapes and on part when there wasn't anything else to do, because in the following week we began with the translation of the documents. Even that same week on the Friday the documents were perused with the interpreter, and when the interpreter left -- sometimes she left earlier -- then we would be looking at videos again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So on which day did you start examining the written documents then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The documents were looked at during the week of the arrest. We started on Friday with an interpreter and that concerned the translation of the newspaper articles, but that particular interpreter was not available any further, and then Monday of the following week Ms. Supput, who had been present during the interview, continued the work of looking at the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, it's convenient to have a lunch break there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will resume at 2.30. (1.00pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 24 25 (2.30pm) (Witness re-enters court) (Interpreter re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbauer, may I remind you you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Turone?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. So the question on which we had the break was on which day you started examining the written documents. You said you started on Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Which Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on 22nd March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: 22nd March. Can you say on which day did you finish the examination of these written documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The analysis with the interpreter was wrapped up on 2nd April, so we were done on 2nd April and my notes were only typed up later, and the whole analysis was done towards the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Right, but remain on the practical examination operation done on these days between March 22nd and April 2nd. So this always together with the interpreter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was always done with the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you proceed exactly in this examination of documents with the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The folders had already been numbered. I said there was the initial "I" for INDA-BAU, "M" for the documents from Mr. Mucic's apartment, and "D" "for the items that had been seized at Taubergasse 15, Door 14, and the folders were given an additional number. The first INDA-BAU folder was given then a I1. So we had numbers 1 through 12. The individual documents were given an additional number. So the first INDA-BAU document had I1/1. Then the others were numbered successively.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you actually proceed in the examination with the interpreter? Did you take the documents one by one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we took one document at a time. The interpreter read out the document and I made notes in handwriting about the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you did not have a written translation done before, before starting this examination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I began with the analysis there was no translation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean the interpreter read out the documents one by one in German translation for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she read the documents and I wrote along.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were all the documents already numbered inside every single folder in which they were contained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The documents -- well, the interpreter was given the document, read it, and then it was given the second number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What do you mean the second number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had an initial "I" and then there is a number depending on which folder it came from, and then thereafter another number was added to the documents. That's the second number, the one after the slash.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see. This was done during the examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the analysis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You took notes during the examining work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you do this work using the original seized documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the originals were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So since you said that work started on March 22nd and ended on April 2nd, you mean you worked every day, even in holidays? How many working days did you sit with the interpreter examining the seized documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eight working days with the interpreter, Friday, then Monday through Friday, and then Monday and Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So eight working days. How many hours every single working day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes the interpreter was in by 8.00, stayed to 4.00. Sometimes she came in at noon and stayed to 4.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon. It would change.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Since you told us that you had also examination of videotapes in the same period of time, did that happen that in the same days you employed extra time to go on examining the videotapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Overtime was put in and in part work was done on the weekends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Was there a time when you recollected all your notes on the seized material and typed them in an organised way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was after all the documents had been examined, after working with the interpreter. The handwritten notes were typed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there a time when you prepared a final report based on these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final report was drafted at the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did this report contain the specific description of the seized items on the basis of your previous notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It includes a short list of the contents and the significant documents are described in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, do you intend to produce his note as part of the evidence? You are going into such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This final report, this is our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is his interpretation of the documents as he understood them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As I understand, we are going to have some more questions about the content of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Has he been designated as an expert? He's interpreting documents. Is he an expert? Has he been designated as such?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Interpretations may differ. That is what his impression of the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The witness has now been talking about description of documents. Anyway, I will go to some other question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I wish I understood where you are going, but if all he did was to collect documents, itemise them and then finally put them into place, I do not see all the force about it other than he described how he took the documents out and the way he preserved them. That is all he tried to show. I'm not interfering with your method of approach. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My goal is to reconstruct in the most complete possible way the work done by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was this final report handed over to the judge of the regional court of Vienna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was handed this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The file was sent by me at the end of April and the report that was finally submitted by the police headquarters to the court, well, I can't tell you exactly what time that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was that handed over to Judge Seda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The papers were transferred to the competent judge. I don't know whether it was Dr Seda or other judges who received this. This was handed over to the competent court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was all the original seized material handed over to the same judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The material was handed to the competent judge. It was Dr Seda. There was also a second judge who dealt with this, Dr Bonet, but I don't know whether he or Dr Seda received these documents. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was the original seized material handed over to the judge on the same day when the final report was handed over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, because my final report with the seized items was handed over to police headquarters in Vienna, which then subsequently transmitted these things to the court. So the headquarters addressed these documents and the seized items to the Vienna District Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you have a direct knowledge of the subsequent delivery of the seized material to some representative of ICTY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was midday, about the 25th May, Sabine Manke came from the Tribunal. She came to our offices and I went to the Vienna District Court, and Dr Bonet, who was the competent judge at the time was handed -- she was handed these objects by this judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you were personally present to this delivery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Miss Sabine Manke receive all the seized material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She received a form listing the seized material and the seized material that was on the form was what she received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She was a witness before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: She was before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did she say she went to collect all that material?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Miss Sabine Manke was a witness before us. I don't recall now whether she was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe when she testified, all she testified was regarding the statement of Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She didn't say she received the documents from the district courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I believe there was no evidence in either direct or cross-examination into that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was this delivery done subsequent to an order issued by the Austrian judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was received from Dr Bonet of the Vienna District Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, we have now the numbering of -- a number of items for purposes of identification from the part of this witness. They are in all 47 items, including seven videotapes, which for reasons of convenience have been already numbered, I believe, by the Registry and which we would like to show the witness for purposes of identification. The binders containing copies of these 47 written documents, including the English transcripts of the seven videotapes are ready and the original items are numbered 104-148. The respective English translations are numbered 104A-148A except for two passports, which do not require any translation. So we have three copies of these binders for your Honours. Of course, the binders are already in the possession of the defence counsel, because counsel has all the seven videotapes besides all the other videotapes which were anyway disclosed to them, and I would ask the binder with the original items be made available to the witness for the purposes of identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I say that we discovered -- first of all, I agree that the Prosecution did bring us a set of these binders and videotapes to be shared among defence counsel. It became necessary for us to look at those this morning. We know the cabinet that they were in, that they were stored in. They have unaccountably disappeared from the defence room. No one seems to know what has happened to them. Fortunately one counsel was able to get a copy made before they disappeared but there is still one copy floating around. I'm not sure that causes any problem particularly, but I just wanted to report to the court that it had happened and somebody had come and removed them from that room and we don't know how and we don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is quite new to us. We gave these binders three weeks ago to all defence lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What he’s saying is they've disappeared. He doesn't say that you did not deliver them. He says they've disappeared from the defence room. I'm sure the Prosecution has got nothing to do with the disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting they did, your Honours. I'm not throwing any stones at the Prosecution at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, you're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a serious matter for the security of this Tribunal. How can things disappear from counsel's room?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We will certainly look into this matter immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The defence room then becomes insecure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It is very surprising and disturbing. I will find what has happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is the second complaint about things happening in that room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Registry will look into this matter immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did I understand that we can anyway proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know with their handicap we should, but it's a very serious complaint and I think it has to be settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I couldn't with a straight face announce a handicap, since there are only a couple of these documents that have anything to do with my client. I think I know which they are and I'm prepared to object to them not having ever seen them, to my knowledge, but I think I know what they are in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, there is also an issue of identification concerning the seven videotapes which are included in these -- among these 47 items. The Prosecution is going to have this witness identify these seven tapes. Of course, not all of the material on this tape is relevant in the submission of the prosecution, and they are actually very, very long. The seven tapes, the total running of the seven tapes, would be about 17 hours, and we -- our submission is the main part of them is actually -- of these 27 -- I mean, 17 hours are actually non-relevant. So in an effort to assist the Chamber and the defence and to move things along, we made excerpts of the parts which the Prosecution considers relevant of these videos and we prepared these excerpts. The total running of the excerpts videos is about two hours and fifteen minutes approximately. Some time ago we gave the defence copies of both the original videos and the excerpts videos, and the transcripts both of the total videos and of the excerpts videos, so that the defence could themselves verify this. Of course, the witness has also seen the videos in original when he examined them, of course, but we had him watch in recent times the seven original tapes in part, and also these seven excerpts videos in part. Thus we will now show during this hearing -- we will seek to show the witness the excerpts of these seven videos, so that he might identify them as coming from the tapes he seized. The excerpting from the seven original videos into seven excerpt videos does not correspond only to a matter of convenience for all of us, but will apply also to the future discussion which will take place in this courtroom as for the admissibility and the relevancy and so on. So we think that we are now going to have all the documents which we seek to tender in future into evidence identified by this witness and also these videos through the watching of the excerpts videos. So we prepared also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you kindly -- have these videos titles?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have they titles?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. They have some titles. They have titles. All the introduction is to say they are going to be handed over to your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can they be identified by their titles?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I will ask some question to this witness right on this point. Since the defence received all the excerpt videos and the original videos, they had anyway the possibility to see how the excerpts correspond to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why is it so difficult for you to answer a simple question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Which is the question, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can't they be identified by their titles?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, they can. "Excerpt video of original video so-and-so". So could we give to the judges also the excerpt videos and excerpt transcripts also? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm at a bit of a loss what the Prosecution -- if I could get the Reader's Digest version ... just from looking at the index of the documents they are purporting to get in through this guy, about half a dozen or one dozen of them are entitled "English translations". Unless somebody can show this man speaks English and presumably Serbo-Croatian, I don't know how he can authenticate an English translation of anything. Like I say, I'm just at an absolute loss where we're heading. If somebody could help me out ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I respond to Mr. Moran? This witness is not supposed to identify an English translation of anything. This witness will be requested to identify some seized documents and within these seized documents there are also seven videotapes. He'll be requested to identify the videotapes both through their external appearance and the labels appearing on them and through watching the videos which he's been examining thoroughly during one week and a half of his working days. About the Reader's Digest, I think that there is a matter of identification which is somehow intermingled with a matter of assessing the relevancy of these videotapes. As I told already the court, the total amount of the seven videotapes, the total running time of the seven videotapes is 17 hours approximately. If the Prosecution should believe that every single minute of these 17 hours were relevant, we would probably consider relevant all the 17 hours of tape, but as a matter of fact we, the Prosecution, from the point of view of the Prosecution, and I'm quite aware that this will be discussed later on, consider relevant, possibly relevant only about two hours and fifteen minutes of these 17 tapes. So the identifying issue intermingles with the relevancy issue in the sense that we are going to ask the witness to identify the tapes, not only through their external appearance, because as a matter of good sense we believe that a tape cannot simply be identified by a mere recognition of the external box containing him. It must be recognised also through the real watching of it. So there is an identifying issue concerning these tapes. On the other hand, the relevancy issue advises us to propose, to suggest to the court and to the defence to show for identification purposes and in view of the quite near discussion on relevancy, to show the parts of the tapes which we, the Prosecution, consider possibly relevant. This is why we are not seeking to show 17 hours of tapes in this courtroom, because we believe that about fifteen, fourteen hours of tapes are non-relevant. Of course, the defence lawyers have the whole tapes. They might use any other part of the tapes which we, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is as if we were not in the same Trial Chamber. They have explained to you the ones given to them have disappeared. Apart from that, are you suggesting that we'll sit here watching all these tapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting -- this is my suggestion, your Honour, that we sit here watching the excerpted parts of these seven videos for identification purposes and in view of the future at the end of this testimony discussion and decision on the relevancy and admissibility of these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I've understood you correctly. The witness stated that these videos were recovered from the property occupied by the two accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All he can say is this excerpt we have obtained was part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The whole tape has to come and becomes part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So relevancy or irrelevancy or admissibility, they do not arise. He says this is a tape that was found there and the excerpt was part of that particular tape, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. He'll only say that this excerpt is part of one of the tapes he could watch personally during the examination work, and he could recognise -- he's supposed to be in a position to recognise these seven videotapes through watching the excerpts of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you take an excerpt, the whole thing has to be admitted into evidence, because an excerpt cannot be taken out of evidence. The whole tape will have to be, because it is talking about relevancy of the rest of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All the tapes -- I might try to be clear. The whole tapes, the whole seven -- the entire seven tapes are going to be -- are seized material and they are the seized items, and the Prosecution is seeking to enter them into evidence entirely simply because the entire item has to be considered a seized item. It wouldn't be proper to cut an original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So all you can say is for your purpose this excerpt is only relevant but the whole has to be part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: They are part of the record. All the videotapes are part of the record. All the videotapes would be entered into evidence for them in reality as identity of original seized items. The excerpts are only a handy device in order to have the videos, first of all, recognised, identified by the witness, and then to give an idea of what is relevant in the submission of the Prosecution in order to aid the future discussion on admissibility and relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You don't talk about relevancy. You say you like on this portion only. The whole thing has to be part of the record. It's not a question of relevancy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a question of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I know. I'm anticipating something which in future will come out. Let us say that our suggestion is to show now the excerpts videos to the witness in order to have them identify the items through a part of them instead of having him and the entire court watch 17 hours of tapes. Of course, I'm not going to start with the tapes. I'm going to start in numbering order according to the index list of the items, but anyway when I'll come to the tapes the problem would come out, so I wanted to explain in advance what is the position and the suggestion of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's a question of not relevancy but reliance on the part of the prosecution. I thought there was a difference between the two, relevancy and your reliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe there is reliance on other portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Of course. I quite agree with your Honour. Anyway, there is now a problem of identification which cannot be resolved simply showing the touchable object of the videotapes to this witness. I see Ms Residovic wants to say something. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I should like to object to this proposal presented by the Prosecution. First of all, in the materials that we have received we have in German and in English reports compiled by the witness. Secondary, in those same materials we have the allegedly confiscated documents in Bosnian and English. It is not clear to me, as to Mr. Moran, what it is that the witness has to identify: his reports in German or documents which were given to us in English and Bosnian, languages which this witness has no understanding of, nor does he seek or write them. Therefore, I am absolutely against the offered exhibits being identified in this way, I'm especially opposed to any kind of identification in the proposed manner because the defence has already during the hearing of the previous witness posed the question of admissibility of these exhibits. We still haven't resolved the question through the examination-in-chief and cross-examination of the witness whether the Prosecution gained possession of various documents that it is giving to the defence occasionally in a lawful manner. Flagrant violations of the manner in which documents are seized can eliminate them from being admitted as evidence regardless of their relevancy. As this question has not been resolved, the presentation of evidence in the Trial Chamber by presenting the contents of that document is absolutely unacceptable and has no grounds in any Rule of this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would seem to me to be a little bit more regular procedure to do this. First, I think they've got a chain of custody problem that's a real problem, where their officers say: "We seized 51 tapes" and the next thing you know there's 54. Presumably German police officers can count up to 54. Then this man watched, he says, 60 tapes over eight business days. Admittedly that goes to the weight, not the admissibility of his testimony, but in all likelihood what occurred is someone here at the Tribunal took these tapes that were shipped from Vienna here and cut them into segments that the Prosecution wants to admit. It seemed to me that the way to do it would be you get the tapes in and then you get the person that made the excerpts off the tapes. It seems to me that would be the more regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He can say a particular excerpt relates to a particular tape. He can say that, because he has seized the tapes and he has already viewed them. He can say: "This particular excerpt relates to this particular tape".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Like I said, that goes to the weight to be given to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That comes later but at this stage we have to have the material that was seized by him in his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He can testify that this tape, number, whatever it is that he put the sticker on, is one that he seized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes. Then he can say: "This excerpt relates to this tape".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or in the alternative whoever made the excerpt can say: "I made the excerpt from this tape". That to me would seem to be the easiest procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have some sympathy for the position that the Prosecution finds themselves in and I think I understand some of the quandary they are facing. It seems to me that the way we have to go about this is by discreet steps. There's no reason for us to sit here and watch seven hours of videotape or 17 hours of videotape or two and a half hours of videotape if the videotape is not admissible before this court in the first place. It seems to me the first step for this Chamber to decide is whether or not the seizure of these documents was lawful in the first place. If this Chamber was to decide that the seizure of these documents was unlawful, then it makes no sense for us to spend all this time sitting here seeing video tapes, playing them and reading the documents seized from those places. The second problem that the Prosecution has is ordinarily when a search is done the documents are marked and identified before they are hauled away from the scene. In this case there were apparently large boxes of material hauled off to the police station and only catalogued and identified at a later time. That creates all kinds of questions about what might have been added and what might be missing. If we get past the first hurdle, then it seems to me the second one is the one to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The witness has stated that one sports bag from Delalic's apartment and a box and some plastic bags were removed in his presence from the premises to the police station, where the inventory was prepared. So we have got the evidence of this witness to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what I am suggesting, your Honour, is we tend to be working backwards. What we are going to do is consider all this evidence and then we'll decide whether or not we should have done that. It seems to me that we should decide whether we should consider it and the Chamber should consider it before we consider it. It is kind of a Lewis Carroll kind of thing: first the punishment, then the trial. I think this Chamber first has to hear the cross-examination of this witness, consider it along with the cross-examination of the other witnesses yesterday, and make a determination whether any of the things that were done by the Austrian police were lawful under the rules of this Tribunal, and once the court -- if the court decides favourably for the Prosecution on that, then we can take this next step, but this may be a total waste of time, if the Tribunal were to agree that what happened in Austria was in violation of the rules of this Tribunal, and that this evidence could not be used because of that. I'm just suggesting a way to maybe do this in a step-by-step fashion that may save us a lot of time in the long run. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, if I may add a few words, I agree with the previous speakers. I should just like to add in relation to this witness and his possible testifying regarding the tapes is simply unacceptable, because the witness can only speak about the authenticity of the tape, and certainly not about the contents of those tapes. He can indeed identify the tape as being A1, 2 or 3, but the contents cannot be identified by this witness in a way that would be relevant for this proceedings. May I also add something that is so well-known, that nowadays equipment is so sophisticated that a video that I can be used in a host of ways. So all he can talk about is the authenticity of the tapes and not the truthfulness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is taking his statement on oath that these documents were recovered from the rooms occupied by Delalic and Mucic and he took them to the police station, where it was prepared. I do not see any difficulty. He has made a statement and notes. You can question him on whether it was a legal seizure. I do not see how he cannot say: "This is a tape that was recovered from the premises of two of the accused". MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, that is the problem that we need to deal with first, the problem mentioned by His Honour Judge Jan. The witness has testified that in a bag and some of the things were brought to the police station, but he was not present when that bag was packed. Apparently there were some 90 tapes collected from other locations and the witness has not testified about that. We also know that there were some video tapes subsequently listed. We don't know which ones they were. These are all matters that we have to resolve through the cross-examination of witnesses. Offering evidence for this trial to see and this witness to see is absolutely unacceptable, because we haven't dealt with the previous issues first. We don't know whether the witness or the Prosecutor gained possession of those documents in a lawful manner. Therefore, our suggestion is that this question of the lawfulness, or rather total unlawfulness, of the seizure of documents should be raised first. Also evidence offered in this way drafted according to the concept of the Prosecutor directly affects my client, Mr. Delalic, and their presentation is actually the presentation of evidence before this Trial Chamber by the Prosecution before they have been admitted as evidence. That is why this procedure is quite unacceptable and contrary to the rules of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We would like to avoid any misunderstanding. We are not now in the stage of admissibility of evidence. We are now on a previous stage of identification of items, and the identification of items must take place at this time. We do not object that any discussion about admissibility in evidence of these items be postponed to after cross-examination, but at this stage we have to be allowed to proceed to the identification stage of every single item. The efforts of the Prosecution is to find out a proper and rational way to have also the seven videotapes identified by this witness and not only the written documents, for instance. For that reason we suggested possibly the playing of the excerpts, but we can even suggest to show not all the excerpts but only a part of it, just enough, either the excerpts or the original tapes, enough as to have the witness say: "Yes, I do remember" or "I don't remember this tape". This can be done also, but in any case it can be done without sound, of course, but we must find out a rational, a reasonable way to have this witness given the possibility to identify the tapes not only by the external appearance but also by something concerning the real content of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you concluded your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If your Honours agree, now I would like to go through the items according to the list, starting from the 1, and having the items submitted to the witness for identification, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If he's in a position to identify them, then he can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If he is in a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If he's not in the position, that will come out, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I, before you do that, mention something of a practical nature? I'm finding the temperature in this room rather oppressive. I can see my learned friend Ms McHenry has been fanning herself for about twenty minutes. I know that Ms McMurrey is feeling uncomfortable. I am finding the temperature in here quite unpleasant, not for any reasons of hot air from counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's quite warm these days.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I just say something about this? We are working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm feeling uncomfortable and I'm not enjoying sitting here at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How do you get the identification done? By the person who properly made them up and the person who can identify the tapes before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In our submission, your Honour, this witness is in a position to identify the items because of what he did with the seized material and according to the description he gave us of the work he has done on that between March and April 1996. So if I'm allowed to go on maybe after the break, since I understand that Ms. McMurrey is not feeling good, I would ask to submit the different items to Mr. Moerbauer for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The documents which he brought from the premises?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The items which are listed in this index. The documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I believe at the police station immediately an inventory was prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. So what they got from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He initialled those tapes. He initialled those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As we could list them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He can identify his initials and say: "This is part of the documents that I bought from the residence of the accused".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The position is if we are not wrong, the witness is in a position to identify the documents and the videotapes which were examined thoroughly by him together with the interpreter as far as the written documents are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is much later. It took him about ten days doing that. As for the documents that were brought to the police station, an inventory must have been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Pardon? What?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As soon as the documents were brought to the police station, an inventory must have been prepared. So on the basis of that inventory he can identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly. This inventory is the big report numbered as document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is much later. I'm talking about the day when these documents were brought. Wasn't at that time an inventory prepared? The report is much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The inventory is the one which was contained in the search records, in the so-called Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: On the basis of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But the witness is probably in a position to identify and recognise these documents through the work he has done, examination and description of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So are you suggesting no inventory was prepared as soon as the documents were brought to the police station? Are you suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The inventory is the one contained in the search records, but being seized --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The copy of the search warrant, only 51 tapes or 28 tapes, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The list contained in the search records was done on the spot on the same day and inevitably very quickly, and the real inventory of such a big amount of material was decided by the Chief of the unit to be done by Mr. Moerbauer in the following days, because it would take a long time to do a real inventory. So we can rely on the memory of Mr. Moerbauer just because he's done a very long work of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't take this for granted. You don't rely on his memory whether, in fact, he took things that day and from the places where he searched. They are both relevant things, and those things which he took from those places where he searched, and there was a list done of those things. Whoever did that, those are the things which we require for the purposes of identification. You could see from your evidence that the documents and the tapes kept on increasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number of documents which were seized is a very big number of documents and the listing which was done in the search records the very day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We are spending too much time discussing things you have carried on without a lot of progress. If he was a member of the team which removed those things, let him identify those things which he removed. That is a simple thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But there's another thing. These documents were seized in response to a request made by foreign authorities so far as the Austrian government was concerned. Why was it necessary for the Austrian government to prepare its own report and to examine these documents? I have not asked the witness. Maybe you can explain. I just want to find that out. It's not necessary to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That was done by the Austrian laws and according to the order of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I can well understand in Austria they want to examine these documents and keep copies, but these things have to be forwarded to a foreign tribunal or authority. Why were they doing an examination of their own and keeping copies of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you want me to ask this question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, I don't want you to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it because you went before an investigating magistrate, because they --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That is the procedure which is followed in -- according to the Austrian law, and I would say in all civil law countries. These items, these documents, these tapes were seized in the framework of an extradition procedure according to Austrian law and from the point of view of Austrian law, and the Austrian authorities consider it necessary to have all these documents described thoroughly, and the description -- the thorough description of these documents could not be done in the very first day, and it took several days, as the witness has explained to us. This was the procedure requested by the investigating judge, Dr Seda, according to the Austrian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I can well understand to find out if a prima facie case is made out before the extradition takes place. Quite right. I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So may I proceed seeking identification of these documents by the part of the witness, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear you. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I object once again. In the testimony the witness said that he was not in Mr. Zejnil Delalic's apartment when the objects were confiscated. He was not in INDA-BAU when those things were seized. He saw those things in a sports bag. He spent one and a half months reviewing, photocopying and so on. Before this witness is cross-examined we cannot allow the identification of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At least he can testify that these documents were in a black -- in a sports bag which he took from the site to the police station. That is what he said. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): He cannot, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Identify the documents -- what was in the sports bag? Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- let me see if I can be of help and put on my amicus hat, if I can. There were seven searches conducted. This man obviously was not at seven different places. I think he can testify that: "I was at location X. I seized this. This is the ones and they were under my control the whole time". He can testify that: "Officer so-and-so gave me these". He cannot say: "These were seized by officer so-and-so pursuant to this search warrant", because he doesn't know. All he knows is these things appeared on his desk in the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No. He carried the sports bag from the site to the police station in the same car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, but that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's what I understand from his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I understand it, there were several searches, and some of these documents came from different searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are only talking about the documents that came from that particular premises -- what's its name? INDA-BAU. We are not talking about documents that came from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I got the impression from the Prosecution that he was going to be testifying about documents seized from all of these locations. I have no problem with him testifying that: "I seized these documents from INDA-BAU".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Or: "I brought the bag containing these documents from the premises to the police station".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As long as we have the chain of custody from the time they were seized to the police station, that is not a problem. If these documents came from somewhere else, he cannot testify they were part of the seizure. Then we are going to have to go through each particular document. Did this come from INDA-BAU where this officer was? If not, then we go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose the evidence is very clear. He knows those ones of which he was responsible for the seizure. It is only in those respects that he can really testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I agree totally, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: But for the time being if he was in custody at all of any document, he's entitled to give evidence identifying those documents which were in his custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: At the time they were in his custody. He cannot testify where they came from or any history to them. He can just say: "On thus and such a date, on 19th March, I obtained custody of these".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That's the most he can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct. We all agree on that, I think, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm sure he is not attempting to say anything different. I know Ms Residovic is concerned about the legality of the seizure itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Admissibility. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I know that the court will bear this in mind. I'm not concerned. I just know that this witness did not confiscate a single document in the apartment or in INDA-BAU. This witness never went to INDA-BAU. He can talk about some carton boxes in the police station in which he may or may not have seen certain documents, but he was not the one who seized those documents. Therefore, he cannot be a witness identifying documents confiscated from Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, if he was not on the site, all he can say is: "These documents were at the police station". If he has been at the search at INDA-BAU, or whatever the name is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think he said INDA-BAU -- then, of course, he can testify as to what he discovered from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I may respond briefly, your Honour, according to the testimony of this witness, and I would say also Mr. Gschwendt, we have a complete chain of custody without any link missing. We have this witness -- we heard that this witness received directly from Mr. Navrat all the materials seized in INDA-BAU, and had it in his custody during the examination period, and then the chain of custody continued without links missing to the delivery to the court, and then we had also the delivery from the court to this Tribunal. So being no missing link in the chain of custody, I don't see any problem with this witness to identify the items which he has been examining thoroughly in a situation of chain of custody without missing links.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I'm being a little dense. What I am used to in chain of custody is Officer A saying: "I seized this kilogram of cocaine. I gave it to Officer B". Officer B says: "I delivered it to the laboratory for testing". Laboratory Technician C says: "I got it from Officer B. I tested it and delivered it to the property room". We seem to be missing the first step: "I've got this kilogram of cocaine". It seems to be missing some place, judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask your Honours to allow me to give the floor for a while to Ms. McHenry about an additional argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: This is just one minute, your Honour. I believe in this Tribunal your Honours can admit any evidence if you find it reliable. There aren't specific rules about hearsay or chain of custody or anything. It's up to your Honours as to what you find is reliable. If this witness explains in detail what was the procedure for the search warrant, who went where and what he received, including from other police officers, and what they told him, it's up to your Honours to believe if that's reliable. I'm very familiar with systems where, for instance, one person is in charge of categorising what is found by other officers, and it's not always the case that every single officer is necessary. Obviously if, after hearing this witness and the arguments, your Honours feel they need to hear other people in the chain of custody, such as Mr. Navrat, we can do that, but I think this Tribunal does not have all these technical rules such that your Honours can make the decision about what you believe is reliable and how things can move expeditiously. Your Honours may decide that you need to hear every single person who was in every single place, but I think it's really up for your Honours and the circumstances, and I believe that at least the Prosecution is entitled to have this officer explain, as he has done, what the procedure was, who was where, and where he received items, including from Mr. Navrat and INDA-BAU. Then it will be up for your Honours to determine if you believe this officer and if the circumstances under which he received the documents from Mr. Navrat are reliable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not a question of any technical rules of evidence. We have to find out how Mr. Navrat obtained the documents, where from he got them. It's not a question of -- you know, we have to be sure that this document -- there is no sort of a -- there's no possibility of these documents having been introduced. He received the documents but from where? From an officer. The officer, where he got them is really important.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I agree with you it's not up to technical rules. What's important is if your Honour feels it's reliable. I think the Prosecution would submit in some circumstances having this officer testify, for instance, that Mr. Navrat gave him a box of documents and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You rely on that portion that he gave to him. From where Mr. Navrat got is not something which he can prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we've had enough. Let me hear Mr. Ackerman and then I close discussion on this. We know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I have no choice but to rise and say that I'm pained to hear what Ms McHenry has to say about this Tribunal, especially considering that she comes from the same legal system that I do. Yes, of course we could do a lot of things more expediently. This case would move along a lot faster if the defendants were not permitted to have counsel. The rules that require a chain of custody of evidence have been developed over more than 200 years of experience, with an understanding that you can't rely on it if you can't have a proper chain of custody. For Miss McHenry to stand up and say to this Tribunal, a world Tribunal, that these are all technicalities and you should ignore them just baffles me. This is a court of justice. I have a great love for justice, and I know this court is here to do justice, not to do the expedient thing. I just want to state for the record that I'm offended by that kind of remark coming from a fellow American.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we have had enough. When we'll come back, we'll come back at 4.30, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will come back at 4.30 and carry on. (3.50 pm) (Short break) (4.35 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly invite the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness appears, may I just have a couple of minutes to respond to something said at the end of -- right before the last break? I believe, given what was said, that it is appropriate that I respond briefly. In particular, I'm responding to the comments of my learned colleague, Mr. Ackerman. I resent the continued attacks on the personal integrity of Prosecution attorneys, including myself. I respectfully submit that such personal attacks are unprofessional and in some cases even unethical, and I would ask the Trial Chamber in the future to stop such attacks. I am not representing any particular country or system. Here, as in my work in the United States, I work for justice, as do my colleagues here from the civil law system. I also state that the comments were an attack on the civil law system also, which my colleagues wish me to stress is over 2000 years old. I finally note that there is nothing improper about suggesting that this Chamber can itself make determinations about what may or may not be admissible and what may or may not be reliable or fairly admitted. Thank you for the opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Frankly I expect counsel generally to be professional and add less trouble to us instead of increasing what we already have. I do not enjoy any iota of disagreement among counsel or counsel and the Trial Chamber. It just does not do anyone any good. I expect as colleagues and as professional colleagues that everything said should relate entirely to the proceedings and in good faith. I'm sure we will not have a repeat of these things any longer. Let us have the witness. (Witness re-entered court) (Interpreter re-entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. May I ask the Registrar to provide the witness then with the binder with the original documents for the purposes of identification please, as I say, 47 items which are numbered 1-47, and as official Exhibit Number 104-148. Of course, the original videotapes are not materially included in these binders, and we'll show them to the witness at an appropriate time. So, Mr. Moerbauer, may I draw your attention to the first document included in the binder? It is a pretty long document written in German language, which is number 104, marked as number 104 for identifying purposes. It is the first document in the binder. Mr. Moerbauer, can you identify this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first document that I see here is a report from the Vienna police to the Vienna District Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is this then your final report containing the description of the seized material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Is this the right one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The first exhibit, numbered as Exhibit Number 104. That's an index actually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have the final report, the analysis of the seized tapes and documents, and the report was made on 24th April, with a summary for the court concerning a summary of the content. That is a report containing the summary of the content of the seized items.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbauer, I see that this final report contains 71 pages in the German language original, but the pages are not numbered from 1-71. Actually it seems to be subdivided into many subsections, and the pages of each subsection are autonomously numbered. I would ask you why didn't you number this big report from page 1 to page 71?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. "Autonomously", what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I would say every single subsection has page numbers 1-3, 1-5, etc, and the general page number then is not entirely 1 until 71. I wanted to ask the

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: 1 to page 71?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At police headquarters we did not number all documents. Each report has its own number system and the continuation of the numbering was carried out by the courts. A report is made and in addition to the report the analyses are added. So they are annexes to the reports, and the reports are classified on a chronological basis by ourselves. That is the order in which they are transferred to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature in this report; I mean in the different subsections of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say briefly how did you classify the seized items in your report? I mean with which initials and which numbering system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The seized items were once again classified under "I" for INDA-BAU; "D" for Taubergasse 15, Door 14; and "M" for Taubergasse 15, Door Number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is the number for the original seized folders reflected in your classifying system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The numbering system used in the report was used from the beginning for the seized items, and it corresponds to what is in the final report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So it is the same system you were talking about in one of the previous questions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In your report you often used the heading "Ausvertung". What do you mean with this word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Ausvertung" is basically a report on the items, that is the content of the documents. So we describe what is transferred to the court and we have seized items, and if these items are required, then the person concerned who has a claim to this can turn to the investigating magistrate and can say in the analysis whether this is of use for the trial of the proceedings or whether they can be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So can you now look at the second document included in the binder, which is number 105 for identification purposes? The second document included in the binder, number 105. That's to say the item number 2 of the binder, after the big report included in the binder. Did you find it, Mr. Moerbauer? Would the Registrar check whether the binders correspond to the index of the document? Probably in the binder you find the English translation too of document 105 or the first document. So I would like you to go to the second item, which is number 105. Did you find that document? Can you identify this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a Yugoslav passport and it was located at Taubergasse 15, Door 10, the apartment of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you find the mention of this document in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just for reasons of simplification, I have a binder here where I have this system listed, and it would be easier for me to locate the same things in this folder. I have made an additional index where I can flick to things more quickly. Maybe I could use this, if you would allow.
